Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
headlines.summary: Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the e-commerce giant's sprawling business operations under CEO Andy Jassy.
headlines.article_text: Amazon memo shows AI coding guidelines, how it tackles tokenmaxxing Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon discouraged teams from relying solely on token usage or code generation as measurements of AI adoption, calling them "deeply flawed" metrics in an internal memo. Companies are grappling with rising AI costs and how to reliably measure whether the tools lead to a boost in productivity. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon CEO Andy Jassy speaks at a company event in New York on Feb. 26, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools. The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI. "We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice." Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs." As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment. Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing , in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks. Read more CNBC tech news A guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectus Nvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone Anthropic's IPO plans: 900% revenue retention, but $80 billion in first-half losses An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks. In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity. It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said. "We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote. Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity. The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said. "Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those." He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation." Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task. "If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo. headlines.article_text: CNBC Workforce Executive Summit 2026 live updates: AI at work Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Mikkelwilliam | E+ | Getty Images Today's workplace faces a litany of challenges. Whether it's shifting power dynamics between employers and employees, the accelerating impact of artificial intelligence on how we work and the skills we need, or the financial stresses that employees of all ranks are feeling, these issues and more are challenging the cohesion of workplace communities. To address these issues, CNBC is convening its premiere council of human resource executives in New York City on Tuesday for the annual CNBC Workforce Executive Summit. The event is exclusive to members of CNBC's Workforce Executive Council. For more about the WEC and to apply for membership, visit www.cnbccouncils.com/wec . 14 Min Ago Steve Cadigan: Mistake companies are making is "using the old tech playbook" watch now VIDEO 4:51 04:51 Steve Cadigan: The real value of AI is in finding ways to create more As AI integrates itself into workplaces, Steve Cadigan, Human Advantage Framework creator and author, told CNBC's Leslie Picker that companies are struggling to realize the promise of the technology. "I think the mistake a lot of us are making is we're using the old tech playbook, which is to use technology to go faster, do more, and save money," he said. "Do I think AI can deliver, go faster, do more, save money? 100% it can. But I think where the real value is is in finding ways to create more." Cadigan pointed out that leadership is more burnt out than ever. "It's an all-time low. I mean, it's blinking red, flat line, code red, and we have a growing level of distrust," he added. He pointed to another decades-old technology — email — that we haven't completely figured out how to leverage for productivity yet either, which should caution executives as to the quick impact that AI could have. "Half of you right now are sitting here going, 'Man, how many emails are we going to have to deal with?' We've weaponized it to get more behind, and so we're walking a million miles an hour towards this AI nirvana, and we haven't even solved email productivity yet." What tech should do, Cadigan said, is "deliver a more beautiful world experience. Isn't that what we want technology for? More beauty, more joy, more time. And now we're seeing more anxiety, more depression, more suicide, more people freaking out." "The creation, the ability for us to create new technology, and that dissonance, I think, is a big, big problem," he added. - Colleen McKown 1 Hour Ago DailyPay's Nelson Chai: On-demand pay can help workers with financial strain watch now VIDEO 2:58 02:58 How companies can help employees stay financially afloat: DailyPay's Nelson Chai Americans are increasingly finding themselves strapped for cash amid the rising costs of groceries, gas and everyday expenses. That is leading more companies to begin to offer earned wage access as a benefit, which allows employees to access money they've already earned ahead of payday Nelson Chai, the CEO of on-demand pay platform DailyPay, told CNBC's Sharon Epperson about how the company's model works. "We have over 2,000 of the largest companies, including many that you've heard of, and we really go in and partner with them," he said. "If you had to wait 14 days to get paid, tomorrow you could go in and you could have access to your wages," he said. Employees are able to access their wages in a few different ways, he said. One option is to use the Daily Pay debit card, another is to do an ACH transfer, and another is to do a transfer to the bank of the employee's choice. "After you've taken out what you want to take out, then we send you the remainder of pay at the time of the normal paycheck," he said. "It's about meeting the workers where they are," he added. - Colleen McKown 1 Hour Ago Digital transformation is “two of the worst words ever used in the history of work” – former LinkedIn CHRO Steve Cadigan When Steve Cadigan was LinkedIn's chief human resources officer, he told CNBC's Leslie Picker at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit that a common trope at the networking platform was that whenever another company announced it was going through a digital transformation, that meant job cuts were on the horizon. "Let's look at all the people in the company that just announced a digital transformation and see who's looking for a new job," Cadigan told Picker. "When you tell employees we're going through a digital transformation, you're basically saying, 'Well, we care about the technology, not about you.'" While companies have heavily invested in AI tools, Cadigan said many have not "built the trust to get people to the point where they can say, 'Yeah, just go ahead and reinvent your job; we got your back.'" As more companies signal AI-driven job cuts, Cadigan said many employees see the first implementation of AI as "cutting people in the name of AI." Instead, Cadigan stressed that organizations need to promise to workers that they are investing in their growth and development, and that while they can't predict how AI will change their jobs or their future employment, these companies will "grow and develop you … we're going to make you a better human being and a better professional, and if things don't work out here, you're going to be a better person on the other side." "That's a bigger promise," he said. — Ian Thomas 2 Hours Ago The CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit is underway! headlines.summary: Companies from Royal Caribbean to Coca-Cola and UPS say they are seeing steady consumer spending despite high inflation.
headlines.article_text: Q3 earnings show resilient U.S. consumer, signs of strain Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Companies from Royal Caribbean to Coca-Cola and UPS say they are seeing steady consumer spending despite high inflation. High fuel prices and interest rates raised concerns about slower consumer spending during the third quarter. Many businesses said they saw resilient spending in the third quarter, though some companies reported weaker sales. In this article KO WHR SHW UPS RCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A customer pushes a shopping cart with cases of Coca Cola outside a Walmart Supercenter retail store in North Bergen, New Jersey, U.S., Nov. 21, 2025. Mike Segar | Reuters One word keeps appearing in third-quarter earnings reports: "resilient." That's the early read on U.S. consumers from various companies that released their results this week. Many businesses say Americans are still spending despite inflationary pressures, though not every company has enjoyed the same success. The commentary comes amid fears that diesel fuel prices, which hit an all-time high of $6.52 per gallon in September, would drive up prices on consumer products . Economists also worried that more expensive regular gas, combined with high borrowing costs and continued tension between the U.S. and Iran, would spur a pullback in consumer spending. Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August. Sales in September were boosted by rising gas station spending. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales. While retail sales rose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August, the September came as gas station spending jumped. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales. "There's been a lot of noise in the market this year. There's a lot of geopolitical stuff," Royal Caribbean Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday. "But I look at our business [and our results], and I think that really talks to the resilience of the business, the resilience of the consumer." Royal Caribbean reported an increase in bookings during its third quarter, while Sherwin-Williams's CEO said the quarter was evidence of the company's strength. Here's how companies are reading the consumer in the most recent three-month period: Coca-Cola The food and beverage company beat analysts' expectations for third-quarter earnings and revenue despite what CEO Henrique Braun called an "uneven environment." Coca-Cola reported that North America unit case volume was flat, indicating demand was steady in the face of higher prices. The company's overall unit case volume was helped by higher demand outside of North America. "The underlying momentum remains quite strong," CFO John Murphy told CNBC. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that." The company increased its full-year forecast and now expects its comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from a prior forecast of growth between 9% and 10%. Royal Caribbean The cruise company beat Wall Street's expectations for earnings per share and narrowly missed on revenue. "Our third quarter results reflect continued strong consumer demand for our vacation experiences and the accelerated momentum across our industry leading brands," CEO Liberty said in the release . The company reported that the number of guests served in the third quarter increased 9% year over year to 2.7 million vacationers and said booking volumes for 2027 were already "up in the high teens," pacing ahead of historical levels and indicating high travel demand. "It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back as relates to the vacation experiences," Liberty told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" following the report. Royal Caribbean shares rose over 8% in Tuesday trading. watch now VIDEO 3:50 03:50 Royal Caribbean CEO Jason Liberty on Q3 earnings beat: We're seeing an uptick in bookings Squawk on the Street Sherwin-Williams Sherwin-Williams beat analysts' expectations for revenue but fell short of expected earnings per share. Sherwin-Williams CEO Heidi Petz said in the company's earnings release that the paint retailer's performance demonstrated "the resilience of our Company and the strength of our strategy in a challenging demand environment." "Despite muted underlying market volumes, we continued to win new customers, increase share-of-wallet and deliver sales growth across all three reportable segments," she said. Net sales increased 7.9% from the same period last year. The company attributed the gain to higher selling prices, but the benefits to profits were partially offset by increased costs of raw materials and supply-chain related expenses. And the company maintained full-year guidance, saying "customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027." UPS A worker drives a United Parcel Service (UPS) truck on Oct. 28, 2025 in Los Angeles, California. Mario Tama | Getty Images UPS beat Wall Street expectations for both earnings per share and revenue in the third quarter. Revenue in the U.S. rose 4.5% during the period to $14.86 billion. CEO Carol Tomé told investors on the company's earnings call that consumers remain "resilient" ahead of the holiday season, the company's busiest period. She said the company expects that average daily shipping volume will grow next quarter at a rate consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume will likely fall due to reducing deliveries with Amazon, she said. UPS has been in the midst of unwinding its partnership with Amazon at the same time it's executing a broad turnaround effort to operate more leanly. The company raised its full-year forecast for the second quarter in a row, projecting consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion. Shares rose more than 4% in Tuesday trading. Whirlpool Not every company is seeing the same spending trends, however. Appliance maker Whirlpool missed on both the top and bottom lines for its third quarter and cut its full-year revenue guidance. Net sales in North America fell more than 8% year over year during the period ending on Sept. 30. Even still, the company cited its own read on "resilience." "Through disciplined working capital management, we are protecting our year end free cash flow and our balance sheet resilience to navigate challenging market conditions," CFO Roxanne Warner said in the earnings release . Shares were down nearly 1% in Tuesday trading. — CNBC's Amelia Lucas and Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report. headlines.summary: Oracle is integrating OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Codex into its applications and plans to add Google TPUs and OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip to OCI.
headlines.article_text: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps, expands cloud chip lineup Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Oracle is adding OpenAI's ChatGPT and Codex to its application stack, extending enterprise access to OpenAI tools. Oracle said OCI will add Google TPUs, OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras hardware as customers seek more silicon options. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk for a keynote at Oracle AI World. In this article OPENAI.FG CBRS ORCL GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable. Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET. For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic , filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering . Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27th, 2026. CNBC Thiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits. "More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release. Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google 's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip. "Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said. It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs. Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers like OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large. OpenAI's Jalapeno chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said. Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday. Read more CNBC tech news A guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectus Nvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone Anthropic's IPO plans: 900% revenue retention, but $80 billion in first-half losses The announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloud Amazon Web Services announced plans to bring Cerebras hardware into its data centers , a major point of validation. Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company. "We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said. A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule. Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital. Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting. Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline. —CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this article Oracle stock chart. watch now VIDEO 10:36 10:36 Watch the full discussion between OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk News Videos Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.

headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: SoFi Technologies, Pentair, Royal Caribbean, JetBlue & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: SOFI, PNR, RCL, JBLU Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Pentair — Shares of the water treatment company leapt 13% after Pentair lifted full-year revenue guidance. Pentair now sees total sales down about 3%, compared to an earlier forecast of 4%-7% decline. Third-quarter results beat on the top and bottom lines. SoFi Technologies — The financial services company jumped 15% after SoFi raised full-year guidance. The company sees revenue totaling $5.04 billion, up from an earlier forecast of $4.75 billion to $4.85 billion, and above the FactSet consensus call for $4.87 billion. SoFi also raised expectations for adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Dell Technologies — The computer and server maker gained 8% after announcing an expansion of its cybersecurity capabilities across artificial intelligence environments. Features include Dell's Resilience Operations for AI service and the PowerProtect AI assistant. AI Infrastructure — Companies providing the backbone of the artificial intelligence build-out climbed Tuesday, helped by improved sentiment after a preliminary filing by Anthropic on Monday to go public and a separate agreement by a group of lenders to finance the purchase of $63 billion in Broadcom technology by Anthropic. Nebius Group surged 11%, Western Digital and Bloom Energy rallied 8% and Astera Labs advanced 9%. Xylem – Shares of the global water tech company sank almost 12%. Xylem cut full-year guidance and now sees adjusted earnings in a range of $5.40 to $5.45 per share, versus an earlier call for $5.55 to $5.70 a share. Profit and revenue in the third quarter also missed the Street's estimates, according to FactSet data. PayPal — Shares rose 2% after the digital payments platform posted third-quarter, bottom-line results that beat estimates. Adjusted earnings of $1.45 per share topped the LSEG consensus estimate of $1.31 per share, and PayPal also lifted its full-year profit forecast. United Parcel Service — The package delivery company gained 3% after reporting third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raising full-year guidance. UPS projects full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from previous expectations of $91.2 billion, and fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion. Nvidia , Meta Platforms — Nvidia said it will invest $3 billion in Meta . The news came after the social media and artificial intelligence giant on Monday announced plans to raise up to $95 billion to support investments in AI infrastructure. Shares of Nvidia gained 1%, while Meta Platforms dipped 0.8%. Royal Caribbean — Shares advanced 8% after RCL reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analyst expectations. The cruise line operator earned $6.57 per share, excluding certain items, topping the LSEG consensus forecast of $6.38 per share. The company also raised full-year earnings guidance for 2026. Boeing — The aerospace company slid 9% after reporting mixed financials for the third quarter . While Boeing posted a wider-than-expected loss, revenue came in above the LSEG consensus estimate. Whirlpool — The appliance maker lost 2% after reporting disappointing earnings and guidance. Whirlpool lost an adjusted 21 cents per share on revenue of $3.68 billion in the third quarter. Analysts were expecting earnings of 80 cents per share on revenue of $3.92 billion, according to LSEG. Whirlpool also cut full-year revenue guidance to $14.5 billion from $15.0 billion. JetBlue Airways — The carrier climbed more than 20% after JetBlue said it expects wider fourth quarter margins even as fuel prices are anticipated to rise 85% above year-earlier levels. JetBlue reported an adjusted loss of 60 cents a share in the third quarter, compared to the 55-cent loss that analysts polled by LSEG had estimated. Revenue narrowly missed expectations, as well. Celestica — The supply chain management company surged 12% after Celestica raised full-year guidance. The company anticipates adjusted earnings of $11.55 per share, up from an earlier forecast of $11.30 a share, above the FactSet consensus forecast for $11.16. Cadence Design Systems — The electronic systems design company rose 8% after third-quarter results surpassed estimates and Cadence raised its full-year revenue growth outlook. Cadence earned $2.11 per share on an adjusted basis and posted revenue of $1.63 billion, while analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected $2.05 per share on $1.61 billion. — CNBC's Scott Schnipper, Ananya Chetia, Michelle Fox, Davis Giangiulio, Fred Imbert, Paulina Likos, Amelia Lucas, Darla Mercado, Laya Neelakandan and Kai Nicol-Schwarz contributed reporting
